lead: Every gas power cycle ends with two questions: how much of the heat comes back as work, and how big must the engine be to deliver that work? Air standard efficiency answers the first — a pure number worked out from the cycle temperatures and γ. Mean effective pressure answers the second — the steady pressure that, pushed through the same swept volume, would give the same net work. Used together they let you compare Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles fairly, and say what is being held equal while you compare.
prereq: You need the four-process gas cycles and their efficiency formulas from Chapter 6.2, the air standard assumptions from Chapter 6.1, and displacement work as a p-v area from Unit 1, Work and heat.

sections.h3: Air standard efficiency: the comparison number

blocks.text: Air standard efficiency is the thermal efficiency of the ideal air cycle, and nothing more. Friction, heat leak and fuel chemistry were removed in Chapter 6.1. Its whole job is comparison: two cycles with the same air standard efficiency would burn the same heat for the same work, if the ideal were all you knew.

blocks.where: η is the air standard efficiency (no unit); w_net is the net work output per kg of air (kJ/kg); q_in is the heat added per kg (kJ/kg); q_out is the heat rejected per kg (kJ/kg).

blocks.text: With constant specific heats, the three cycles of Chapter 6.2 give:

blocks.where: r = v1/v2 is the compression ratio, the volume before compression divided by the volume after; γ = cp/cv is the ratio of specific heats, about 1.4 for air.
rc = v3/v2 is the cut-off ratio, the volume at the end of constant pressure heat addition divided by the volume at the start of it.
rp = p3/p2 is the pressure ratio of the constant volume part of the heat addition; rc is the cut-off ratio of the constant pressure part.

blocks.text: Specific work is w_net in kJ/kg. The work ratio is net work divided by positive work: wr = 1 − w_comp / w_exp, where w_exp is the expansion work and w_comp the compression work, both in kJ/kg. A low work ratio means a big machine for a small output, so gas turbines watch it closely.

sections.h3: Mean effective pressure: the size number

blocks.text: Mean effective pressure, MEP, tells you how hard the engine works for each cubic metre of cylinder it sweeps.

blocks.where: w_net is the net work per kg (kJ/kg); v1 and v2 are the specific volumes at the start and end of compression (m³/kg); v1 − v2 is the swept volume per kg of air.

blocks.text: Watch the units. kJ/kg divided by m³/kg gives kN/m², which is kPa. Divide by 100 for bar.

On the p-v diagram the net work is the enclosed area (Unit 1, displacement work). Draw a rectangle of the same area with width v1 − v2; its height is the MEP. So MEP is the constant pressure that, acting through the whole stroke, would do the same work as the real, rising and falling pressure. Engines are sized by displacement, so MEP is work per unit of engine size — the fair way to compare machines.

A bigger MEP from the same swept volume means a smaller, lighter engine for the same power. Real full-load values are of the order of 10 bar, so an ideal-cycle answer of a few bar up to some tens of bar is believable.

MEP rises with r at fixed heat input. The swept volume per kg, v1(1 − 1/r), does grow with r at fixed v1, which by itself would lower MEP. But the efficiency rises faster in percentage terms, so the net work per kg grows faster than the swept volume and MEP rises.

sections.h3: Comparing the cycles: two fair questions

blocks.text: Two comparisons exist, and they crown opposite winners. Always say which one you are answering.

Same compression ratio. At a given r, Otto is highest, Dual next, Diesel lowest. The figure shows this at γ = 1.4 with the Diesel at rc = 2 and the Dual at rp = 1.5, rc = 2. The reason is the temperature at which heat enters. The efficiency of any reversible cycle is 1 − T_out,mean / T_in,mean, where T_in,mean is the mean temperature at which heat is supplied and T_out,mean is the mean temperature at which heat is rejected (Unit 3, Carnot's theorem). Constant volume addition puts the heat in at the top of compression, so the mean temperature of heat supply is highest: each kJ added raises T by 1/cv. Constant pressure addition raises it more slowly, by 1/cp per kJ, because part of the heat goes into expansion work. So for the same heat input at the same r the mean temperature of heat supply is lower, and less of the heat becomes work.

Same maximum pressure and temperature. Now Diesel is highest, Dual next, Otto lowest. This is the real design limit, because pistons, valves and the cylinder head are limited by peak pressure and peak temperature. A diesel compresses air alone to a high r and then adds heat slowly, so it can run at r = 16 to 22 while keeping the peak inside the metal's limit. A petrol engine must add all its heat at the top of compression, so raising r raises the peak sharply and causes knock. That is why petrol engines stay near r = 8 to 12, and the diesel wins in practice even though it loses the same-r comparison.
Effect of γ. A larger γ raises η for every cycle, because r^(γ−1) grows faster. A monatomic gas such as argon (γ = 1.67) would beat air (γ = 1.4). Exhaust gas left in the cylinder lowers γ a little.

Effect of rc. At fixed r, a longer constant pressure burn (larger rc) lowers Diesel efficiency, because more heat enters at falling temperature. Real diesels keep rc near 2 and get their efficiency from high r instead. Rate of pressure rise and peak pressure limit rc.

figure.caption: Air standard efficiency against compression ratio at γ = 1.4. At any given r, Otto is the top curve; the Diesel (rc = 2) and Dual (rp = 1.5, rc = 2) curves sit below it because part of their heat enters at constant pressure.

spec.aria: Three efficiency curves rising with compression ratio, with Otto highest, Dual in the middle and Diesel lowest at the same compression ratio.

examples.question: An ideal Otto cycle takes air at p1 = 1 bar and T1 = 300 K, with a compression ratio of 8. The net work is 451.8 kJ/kg. Take R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Find (a) the specific volume at the start of compression, (b) the specific volume at the end of compression, (c) the mean effective pressure in kPa and in bar.
steps: Convert the pressure to kPa: p1 = 1 bar = 100 kPa.
Treat air as an ideal gas at state 1: v1 = R T1 / p1 = 0.287 × 300 / 100 = 86.1 / 100 = 0.861 m³/kg.
Compression ratio r = v1 / v2 = 8, so v2 = v1 / 8 = 0.861 / 8 = 0.1076 m³/kg.
Swept volume per kg = v1 − v2 = 0.861 − 0.1076 = 0.7534 m³/kg.
examples.answer: v1 = 0.861 m³/kg, v2 = 0.1076 m³/kg, and the mean effective pressure is 599.7 kPa, about 6.0 bar.
examples.check:
R = 0.287
T1 = 300.0
p1 = 100.0
r = 8.0
w = 451.8
v1 = R * T1 / p1
v2 = v1 / r
mep = w / (v1 - v2)
print(round(v1, 3))
print(round(v2, 4))
print(round(mep, 1))
print(round(mep / 100, 2))

traps: Dividing w_net by v1 instead of the swept volume v1 − v2. At r = 8 that gives 524.7 kPa instead of 599.7 kPa — about 12% low, because MEP is work per unit swept volume.
Comparing cycles without saying what is fixed. At the same r, Otto wins; at the same peak pressure and temperature, Diesel wins.
Unit slip: kJ/kg ÷ m³/kg gives kPa, not bar. Divide by 100 at the end, not at the start.
Quoting air standard efficiency as the brake efficiency of a real engine; the real value is 20 to 30 percentage points lower.
Feeding r into the Diesel formula where rc belongs, or using γ = 1.4 for a gas that is not air.

quiz.q: Define air standard efficiency and write the Otto formula.
quiz.a: η = w_net/q_in = 1 − q_out/q_in, where w_net is net work per kg and q_in, q_out are the heat added and rejected per kg. For Otto, η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1), with r the compression ratio and γ = cp/cv.

quiz.q: Why does constant volume heat addition give a higher efficiency than constant pressure addition at the same compression ratio?
quiz.a: Efficiency is 1 − T_out,mean/T_in,mean. Constant volume addition puts the heat in at the top of compression, raising T by 1/cv per kJ, so T_in,mean is highest. Constant pressure addition raises T more slowly, by 1/cp per kJ, because part of the heat becomes expansion work; for the same heat input T_in,mean is lower and less of the heat becomes work.

quiz.q: An Otto cycle has r = 10, v1 = 0.9 m³/kg and w_net = 600 kJ/kg. Find the mean effective pressure in kPa and bar.
A Diesel cycle runs at r = 16 and rc = 2 with γ = 1.4. Find its air standard efficiency.
A four-stroke engine of 2 litre swept volume runs at 3000 rev/min with a mean effective pressure of 8 bar. Find the power.
quiz.a: 8 bar = 800 kPa, swept volume 0.002 m³, so work per cycle = 800 × 0.002 = 1.6 kJ. A four-stroke fires once per two revolutions: 3000/60/2 = 25 cycles per second. Power = 1.6 × 25 = 40 kW.

quiz.q: At the same maximum pressure and temperature, why does the Diesel cycle beat the Otto cycle even though it loses at the same compression ratio?
quiz.a: Peak pressure and temperature limit the metal. The diesel compresses air only, so it can use a much higher r for the same peak, then adds heat at constant pressure while staying at the limit. The Otto cycle must add all its heat at the top of compression, so its r is capped — in practice by knock — well below the diesel's. The higher r more than pays for its lower-efficiency heat addition.

quiz.q: Why does MEP rise with compression ratio at fixed heat input?
quiz.a: w_net = η q_in rises with r, and the swept volume per kg v1(1 − 1/r) also rises, but the efficiency gain outpaces it, so net work per cubic metre swept still rises.

beyond: Not for the exam. Test cells log MEP directly: a pressure transducer gives the indicator diagram, and its area divided by the swept volume is the indicated mean effective pressure (IMEP). Brake MEP subtracted from IMEP gives friction MEP, a standard way to track engine wear. Simulation tools report MEP because it maps straight onto torque, and the same idea is reused for Stirling engines and fuel cells as work per unit displacement.
